query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Implementing a phase‐selective recrystallization treatment via tailored annealing will selectively recrystallize the ductile phase within the dual‐phase lamellar eutectic high-entropy alloy, reducing dislocation pile-ups at phase boundaries and thereby overcoming limited room-temperature tensile ductility while retaining or even increasing strength.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar (ductile and strong phases) microstructure exhibiting dislocation accumulations at internal boundaries that cause local stress concentrations and premature microcracking.
generation.intervention: A single tailored annealing process designed to trigger phase-selective recrystallization of the soft (ductile) phase without disturbing the integrity of the hard phase framework.
generation.conditions: Processing under controlled heating at a temperature and duration optimized to initiate recrystallization of the ductile phase at room temperature conditions without full homogenization. Tensile testing should be performed at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined and more uniform distribution of the recrystallized ductile phase that smooths the internal phase boundaries, thereby mitigating dislocation pile-ups and lowering local stress concentrations.
generation.mechanism: The selective recrystallization reduces the inhomogeneous accumulation of dislocations near the internal interfaces, lowering local stress and delaying microcrack initiation. This enables higher strain hardening and more uniform deformation, leading to enhanced ductility with preserved or increased strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: An observable increase in uniform tensile elongation (improved ductility) coupled with retained or slightly increased high tensile strength compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic alloy, which is characterized by its dual-phase lamellar microstructure and limited room-temperature ductility due to stress concentrations from dislocation pile-ups at the phase interfaces.
generation.boundary: The success of the intervention depends critically on the precise control of annealing temperature and time; excessive recrystallization or uneven treatment may weaken the strong phase network and compromise strength.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in ductility and strength are not precisely predictable and will depend on the processing window. Long-term stability and fatigue behavior after the intervention also remain to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples: one set subjected to the tailored phase-selective recrystallization annealing and one untreated control set. Perform room-temperature tensile tests and detailed microstructural analyses (using TEM and SEM) to compare dislocation distributions and phase morphology.
measurements: Tensile stress-strain curves to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and uniform elongation
High-resolution TEM/SEM imaging to assess the degree of recrystallization in the ductile phase and the presence of dislocation pile-ups at the phase interfaces
Microhardness mapping across the lamellar colonies
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in ductility (uniform elongation) and reduction in dislocation pile-ups compared to the control, or if the tensile strength is markedly reduced, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution and a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure, exhibited the combination of both high fracture strength and high ductility, which has never been achieved in previously reported HEAs. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. cited_evidence.text: The quest for improved damage tolerance drives the development of new high-strength high-toughness materials, e.g. dual-phase HEAs, advanced (such as dual-phase, twinning-induced plasticity - TWIP, transformation induced plasticity - TRIP) steels, Ti- and Cu-alloys. The growing interest in dual-phase HEAs and in FeCoCrNiAlx alloys in particular has valid reasons. For instance, the FeCoCrNiAl alloy can be regarded as a lightweight dual-phase high entropy superalloy with potential for high-temperature structural applications, e.g. aerospace engine components. Owing to its high Fe and Al contents, FeCoCrNiAl is lighter and cheaper to fabricate than conventional super-alloys. Other varieties containing Ti in addition demonstrated excellent room temperature compressive strengths that were superior even to many bulk metallic glasses. To date FeCoCrNiAlx alloys have been studied mostly in terms of their metallurgy and basic mechanical quantities,,,. Their microstructure and constitution of phases are very sensitive to the Al content and can be purposely varied from single-phase fcc (for x ≅ 0–0.4), to dual-phase fcc + bcc/B2 (for x ≅ 0.4–0.9) to single-phase bcc/B2 (for x ≅ 0.9–2.0),,.

In conclusion, we proposed a universal routine of PSR to ductilize eutectic alloys. The PSR, i.e., individual recrystallization of the soft phase and recovery of the hard phase, was achieved by tailoring the strain partitioning behavior between the two phases of eutectics. Compared with traditional processing methods for eutectic alloys, the PSR prevents premature fracture by eliminating the weak boundaries and thus triggers the intrinsically superior strain hardening capacity of the two phases through dislocation multiplication and potential phase transformation. In a typical FCC/B2 EHEA, ∼35% uniform elongation and ∼2 GPa true stress were achieved. The strain partitioning-dominated PSR mechanism ensures its good adaptability in other duplex alloys, as proven in the A357 alloy. This strategy will open new frontiers of eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials in model civilization by combining their excellent castability and strengthening capacity.
